content.text:
Several events repeat after fixed intervals. When will they happen together again?

The key idea is:

If the intervals are t1, t2, t3, ...

the next common occurrence comes after the L.C.M. of those intervals.

Why? Because the elapsed time must be a multiple of every interval at the same time.
Three events repeat every 6 s, 8 s and 12 s. After how much time will they next occur together?

hints: The elapsed time must be divisible by all three intervals.
Because we want the first common time, use the L.C.M.
inlineData.prompt: Three events repeat every 6 s, 8 s and 12 s. After how much time will they next occur together?
inlineData.explanation: Correct. L.C.M.(6, 8, 12) = 24 seconds.

content.text:
The common time must be a common multiple of 6, 8 and 12.

The least common multiple is:

L.C.M.(6, 8, 12) = 24

So they next occur together after 24 seconds.

Book example: three traffic lights change every 48 s, 72 s and 108 s.

They all change together at 8:20:00.

First find the common interval:

L.C.M.(48, 72, 108) = 432 seconds

Convert:

432 seconds = 7 minutes 12 seconds

So the next common change is:

8:20:00 + 7:12 = 8:27:12

The L.C.M. gives elapsed time; the starting clock time comes afterward.
If traffic lights change every 48 s, 72 s and 108 s and start together at 8:20:00, when do they next change together?

hints: Convert 432 seconds to minutes and seconds before adding it.
inlineData.prompt: If traffic lights change every 48 s, 72 s and 108 s and start together at 8:20:00, when do they next change together?
inlineData.explanation: Correct. 432 seconds = 7 minutes 12 seconds, so 8:20:00 + 7:12 = 8:27:12.

content.text:
L.C.M.(48, 72, 108) = 432 seconds.

432 = 7 × 60 + 12

So the interval is 7 minutes 12 seconds.

8:20:00 + 7:12 = 8:27:12
Traffic lights change every 45 s, 75 s and 90 s. If they change together at 7:20:15, when will they next change together?

inlineData.prompt: Traffic lights change every 45 s, 75 s and 90 s. If they change together at 7:20:15, when will they next change together?

content.text:
The book's later traffic-light question uses 45, 75 and 90 seconds.

L.C.M. = 450 seconds.

450 seconds = 7 minutes 30 seconds.

Starting at 7:20:15:

7:20:15 + 7:30 = 7:27:45.

Good. The pattern is now automatic:

fixed intervals → L.C.M. → elapsed common time → add to the starting clock time.

Before taking an L.C.M., all intervals must be expressed in one common unit.

For this chapter:

1 minute = 60 seconds
1 hour = 60 minutes = 3600 seconds

For example:

30 minutes = 30 minutes
1 hour = 60 minutes
1.5 hours = 90 minutes
1 hour 45 minutes = 105 minutes

Now the intervals are ready for one L.C.M. calculation.
For intervals of 30 min, 1 hour, 1.5 hours and 1 hour 45 min, which unit is most convenient before finding the L.C.M.?

hints: Convert every interval to the same unit.
inlineData.prompt: For intervals of 30 min, 1 hour, 1.5 hours and 1 hour 45 min, which unit is most convenient before finding the L.C.M.?
inlineData.explanation: Correct. The convenient common-unit set is 30, 60, 90 and 105 minutes.

content.text:
Use minutes:

30 min
1 hour = 60 min
1.5 hours = 90 min
1 hour 45 min = 105 min

Then take the L.C.M. of 30, 60, 90 and 105.

Book example: four devices beep after 30 min, 1 hour, 1.5 hours and 1 hour 45 min.

Convert to minutes:

30, 60, 90, 105

The book finds:

L.C.M. = 1260 minutes

1260 minutes = 21 hours.

If they all beep together at 12 noon, the next common time is:

12 noon + 21 hours = 9 a.m. the next day.
Four devices beep every 30, 60, 90 and 105 minutes and start together at 12 noon. When will they next beep together?

inlineData.prompt: Four devices beep every 30, 60, 90 and 105 minutes and start together at 12 noon. When will they next beep together?
inlineData.explanation: Correct. L.C.M. = 1260 min = 21 h, so the next common beep is 9 a.m. the next day.

content.text:
L.C.M.(30,60,90,105) = 1260 minutes.

1260 minutes = 21 hours.

Starting at noon, 21 hours later is 9 a.m. the next day.

For runners on one circular track, use the time for one complete revolution as each interval.

If a runner needs 54 seconds for one round, every 54 seconds that runner returns to the starting point.

All runners are together at the starting point again when the elapsed time is a common multiple of all revolution times.

So again:

meeting time = L.C.M. of revolution times.

Book solved example:

Seema, Meena and Reema complete one revolution in:

54 s
42 s
63 s

The source finds:

L.C.M.(54,42,63) = 378 s

378 s = 6 min 18 s

Therefore they meet again at the starting point after 6 minutes 18 seconds.
Three runners complete one round in 54 s, 42 s and 63 s. After how much time will they all return together to the starting point?

hints: Then convert 378 seconds to minutes and seconds.
inlineData.prompt: Three runners complete one round in 54 s, 42 s and 63 s. After how much time will they all return together to the starting point?
inlineData.explanation: Correct. 378 seconds = 6 minutes 18 seconds.

content.text:
L.C.M.(54,42,63) = 378 seconds.

378 = 6 × 60 + 18

So the answer is:

6 min 18 sec.

Another source-backed example uses round times:

24 s, 36 s and 48 s.

L.C.M.(24,36,48) = 144 seconds

144 seconds = 2 minutes 24 seconds.
Three girls complete one round in 24 s, 36 s and 48 s. After how much time will they meet at one point?

hints: Find the L.C.M. of the three round times.
inlineData.prompt: Three girls complete one round in 24 s, 36 s and 48 s. After how much time will they meet at one point?
inlineData.explanation: Correct. L.C.M.(24,36,48) = 144 seconds = 2 minutes 24 seconds.

content.text:
L.C.M.(24,36,48) = 144 seconds.

144 seconds = 2 minutes 24 seconds.

So they next meet after 2 minutes 24 seconds.

The chapter also includes fractional revolution times.

The source uses:

91/6 seconds
65/4 seconds
56/3 seconds

To handle these, the chapter applies its fraction L.C.M. rule:

L.C.M. of fractions
= L.C.M. of numerators / H.C.F. of denominators

So:

L.C.M.(91/6,65/4,56/3)
= L.C.M.(91,65,56) / H.C.F.(6,4,3)
= 3640 seconds

3640 seconds = 1 hour 40 seconds.
For 91/6 s, 65/4 s and 56/3 s per revolution, what common return time does the source obtain?

hints: Use the fraction L.C.M. rule from the chapter.
The source's final result is 3640 seconds.
inlineData.prompt: For 91/6 s, 65/4 s and 56/3 s per revolution, what common return time does the source obtain?
inlineData.explanation: Correct. The source gets 3640 seconds = 1 hour 40 seconds.

content.text:
Use:

L.C.M.(91,65,56) / H.C.F.(6,4,3)

The source obtains:

3640 seconds

= 3600 + 40
= 1 hour 40 seconds.

Another source-backed stadium example gives round times:

252 s
308 s
198 s

The source finds:

L.C.M.(252,308,198) = 2772 s

Convert:

2772 = 46 × 60 + 12

So they meet again at the common starting point after:

46 min 12 sec.
Runners take 252 s, 308 s and 198 s per round. When do they next meet at the starting point?

inlineData.prompt: Runners take 252 s, 308 s and 198 s per round. When do they next meet at the starting point?
inlineData.explanation: Correct. 2772 seconds = 46 minutes 12 seconds.

content.text:
L.C.M.(252,308,198) = 2772 seconds.

2772 - 2760 = 12
2760 seconds = 46 minutes

So:

2772 seconds = 46 min 12 sec.

The chapter also asks how many simultaneous events occur during a fixed duration.

There is one important counting convention:

When all events start together at time zero, the initial simultaneous event is included.

So if:

common interval = T
duration = D

and D is exactly a whole number of T intervals, the chapter counts:

D/T + 1

The +1 is the starting event at time zero.
If events occur together at time 0 and every 10 seconds afterward, how many simultaneous occurrences are counted during 30 seconds?

hints: The initial event at time zero is counted.
inlineData.prompt: If events occur together at time 0 and every 10 seconds afterward, how many simultaneous occurrences are counted during 30 seconds?
inlineData.explanation: Correct. The occurrences are at 0, 10, 20 and 30 seconds: 4.

content.text:
The times are:

0 s
10 s
20 s
30 s

So there are 4 simultaneous occurrences.

This is why the chapter uses:

D/T + 1

when D is an exact multiple of T and the initial event is included.

Book objective example:

Six bells toll at intervals of:

2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12 seconds.

First:

L.C.M.(2,4,6,8,10,12) = 120 seconds

So they toll together every 120 seconds.

Thirty minutes = 1800 seconds.

Number of complete 120-second intervals:

1800/120 = 15

Include the starting toll:

15 + 1 = 16

So the book's answer is 16 simultaneous tolls.
Six bells start together and toll every 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12 s. How many times do they toll together in 30 min?

hints: Use the common interval 120 s and include the initial toll.
inlineData.prompt: Six bells start together and toll every 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12 s. How many times do they toll together in 30 min?

content.text:
Common interval:

L.C.M.(2,4,6,8,10,12) = 120 s

Duration:

30 min = 1800 s

So:

1800/120 = 15 intervals

Plus the initial event:

15 + 1 = 16.

Next source-backed example:

Four bells toll at:

6 s
7 s
8 s
9 s

Common interval:

L.C.M.(6,7,8,9) = 504 s

Duration:

1.54 hours = 1.54 × 3600 = 5544 s

Number of complete intervals:

5544/504 = 11

Include the initial event:

11 + 1 = 12

So the source gives:

12 times, at a common interval of 504 seconds.
Four bells toll every 6, 7, 8 and 9 seconds. In 1.54 hours, how many times do they toll together and what is the interval?

inlineData.prompt: Four bells toll every 6, 7, 8 and 9 seconds. In 1.54 hours, how many times do they toll together and what is the interval?
inlineData.explanation: Correct. Common interval = 504 s and the count including the initial event is 12.

content.text:
Compute:

L.C.M.(6,7,8,9) = 504 s

1.54 hours = 5544 s

5544/504 = 11

Including the initial toll:

11 + 1 = 12

Keep elapsed time and clock time separate.

If the common interval is 450 seconds, that means the next coincidence is 450 seconds after the starting event.

Only after finding the interval do we add it to a clock time.

So:

450 s = 7 min 30 s

Starting at 7:20:15:

7:20:15 + 7:30 = 7:27:45
If the common interval is 450 seconds and all events coincide at 7:20:15, what is the next coincidence time?

inlineData.prompt: If the common interval is 450 seconds and all events coincide at 7:20:15, what is the next coincidence time?
inlineData.explanation: Correct. 450 seconds = 7 minutes 30 seconds, giving 7:27:45.

content.text:
450 seconds = 7 minutes 30 seconds.

Then:

7:20:15 + 0:07:30 = 7:27:45.

The source also includes a simple repeated-group problem:

Seeta makes necklaces using exactly 16, 20 or 36 beads, with none left over.

The least possible total must be divisible by all three.

So:

Required total = L.C.M.(16,20,36) = 720 beads.

This is not a clock question, but the same common-multiple idea is underneath it.
What is the least number of beads that can be grouped exactly into necklaces of 16, 20 or 36 beads?

hints: The total must be a common multiple of 16, 20 and 36.
inlineData.prompt: What is the least number of beads that can be grouped exactly into necklaces of 16, 20 or 36 beads?

content.text:
L.C.M.(16,20,36) = 720.

So 720 is the least total that can be divided exactly into groups of 16, 20 or 36.

The wheels problem is different because the source gives revolutions per minute, not seconds per revolution.

Three wheels make:

40 rpm
24 rpm
16 rpm

There is a red spot on each wheel, all touching the ground together at time zero.

First convert RPM into time for one revolution.

Formula used here:

time for one revolution = 60 seconds / revolutions per minute.

Convert each wheel:

40 rpm:
60/40 = 3/2 seconds per revolution

24 rpm:
60/24 = 5/2 seconds per revolution

16 rpm:
60/16 = 15/4 seconds per revolution

Now it is a common-period problem for:

3/2 s, 5/2 s and 15/4 s.

The source uses the fraction L.C.M. rule:

L.C.M. = L.C.M. of numerators / H.C.F. of denominators

So:

L.C.M.(3/2,5/2,15/4)
= L.C.M.(3,5,15) / H.C.F.(2,2,4)
= 15/2 seconds
= 7.5 seconds
= 7 1/2 seconds.
Three wheels rotate at 40, 24 and 16 revolutions per minute. When do their marked spots next touch the ground together?

hints: Convert RPM to seconds per revolution first.
Then use the fraction L.C.M. rule.
inlineData.prompt: Three wheels rotate at 40, 24 and 16 revolutions per minute. When do their marked spots next touch the ground together?
inlineData.explanation: Correct. The source converts to 3/2, 5/2 and 15/4 seconds per revolution and gets 15/2 = 7.5 seconds.

content.text:
Do not take the L.C.M. of 40, 24 and 16 directly.

These are rates.

First convert:

40 rpm → 3/2 s
24 rpm → 5/2 s
16 rpm → 15/4 s

Then:

L.C.M. = 15/2 = 7 1/2 seconds.

The pendulum problem is the most specialized cyclic example in this chapter.

The source states:

First pendulum: 5 strikes in 3 seconds
Second pendulum: 7 strikes in 4 seconds

The source interprets the intervals as:

3/5 second
4/7 second

Then it applies the fraction L.C.M. rule:

L.C.M.(3/5,4/7)
= L.C.M.(3,4) / H.C.F.(5,7)
= 12 seconds

So, according to the source solution, they strike together every 12 seconds.
According to the chapter's solution, how often do the two pendulums strike together?

hints: Follow the chapter's stated interpretation of the strike rates.
Apply the fraction L.C.M. rule to 3/5 and 4/7.
inlineData.prompt: According to the chapter's solution, how often do the two pendulums strike together?
inlineData.explanation: Correct. The source obtains a common interval of 12 seconds.

content.text:
The source uses:

3/5 second
4/7 second

Then:

L.C.M.(3,4) / H.C.F.(5,7)
= 12/1
= 12 seconds

So the source answer is 12 seconds.

Now count clear strikes in 1 minute using the source's method.

First pendulum:

60 × 5/3 = 100 strikes

Second pendulum:

60 × 7/4 = 105 strikes

Total individual counts:

100 + 105 = 205

They strike together every 12 seconds.

The source counts simultaneous strike moments in 1 minute as:

60/12 + 1 = 6

because the initial simultaneous strike is included.

Those 6 moments were counted in both 100 and 105, so subtract 6 once:

205 - 6 = 199 clear strikes.
A pendulum strikes 5 times in 3 seconds and another 7 times in 4 seconds. If both start together, how many clear strikes are heard in 1 minute?

hints: Subtract the 6 simultaneous strike moments counted twice.
inlineData.prompt: A pendulum strikes 5 times in 3 seconds and another 7 times in 4 seconds. If both start together, how many clear strikes are heard in 1 minute?
inlineData.explanation: Correct. The source gives 100 + 105 - 6 = 199 clear strikes.

content.text:
Source method:

100 strikes from the first
105 strikes from the second

Total = 205

Common strikes every 12 s:

60/12 + 1 = 6

Clear strikes:

205 - 6 = 199

The source also gives three persons with fractional times for one complete revolution:

91/6 s
65/4 s
56/3 s

and obtains:

L.C.M. of the periods = 3640 s

= 1 hour 40 seconds.

The lesson here is simple:

When a cyclic interval is fractional, keep the physical meaning first — 'time for one cycle' — and then use the fraction L.C.M. rule from the chapter.

At this point, the situations may look different, but the recognition pattern is the same.

Traffic lights:
intervals in seconds → L.C.M. → add to starting time.

Electronic devices:
convert minutes/hours → L.C.M. → add to starting time.

Runners:
time per revolution → L.C.M. → common return.

Wheels:
RPM → time per revolution → fraction L.C.M.

Bells:
L.C.M. → common interval → count simultaneous events, including the initial event as the chapter does.

Pendulums:
follow the source's rate-to-interval interpretation → common interval → count strikes → remove overlap.
What is the main quantity that determines the next time several fixed-interval repeating events coincide?

hints: Think 'first common multiple' of all the intervals.
The intervals must all divide the elapsed common time.
inlineData.prompt: What is the main quantity that determines the next time several fixed-interval repeating events coincide?
inlineData.explanation: Correct. The next simultaneous occurrence is governed by the L.C.M. of the repeating intervals.

content.text:
The events coincide again when the elapsed time is divisible by every interval.

The first such elapsed time is their L.C.M.

So:

fixed repeating intervals → L.C.M.
Six bells have a common interval of 120 seconds. Over 1800 seconds, using the chapter's initial-event convention, how many simultaneous tolls are counted?

hints: Add one for the initial event at time zero.
inlineData.prompt: Six bells have a common interval of 120 seconds. Over 1800 seconds, using the chapter's initial-event convention, how many simultaneous tolls are counted?
inlineData.explanation: Correct. 1800/120 = 15 intervals, plus the initial simultaneous toll = 16.

content.text:
1800/120 = 15 complete common intervals.

The source's convention includes the initial occurrence:

15 + 1 = 16.
A wheel rotates at 40 revolutions per minute. What is its time for one revolution?

inlineData.prompt: A wheel rotates at 40 revolutions per minute. What is its time for one revolution?
inlineData.explanation: Correct. One revolution takes 60/40 = 3/2 seconds.

content.text:
At 40 revolutions per minute:

60 seconds / 40 revolutions
= 3/2 seconds per revolution.

That period, not the RPM itself, is used in the cyclic L.C.M. calculation.

Excellent work.

You now have the complete cyclic-event framework from this chapter:

Core rule:
fixed repeating intervals → next simultaneous occurrence after their L.C.M.

Starting-time problems:
find the common interval first, then add it to the given clock time.

Unit conversion:
make all intervals use the same unit before taking the L.C.M.

Traffic lights and electronic devices:
L.C.M. gives the elapsed common interval.

Circular runners:
use the time for one revolution as each repeating interval, then take the L.C.M.

Fractional revolution times:
use the chapter's fraction L.C.M. rule.

Wheels:
first convert revolutions per minute into seconds per revolution:
60/RPM

Then take the L.C.M. of the resulting periods.

Counting:
for a duration containing D/T whole common intervals, the chapter includes the starting simultaneous event, giving D/T + 1.

Bells:
use that counting convention directly.

Pendulums:
follow the source's stated conversion of strike rates into intervals, find the common interval, count individual strikes, and subtract simultaneous overlap once to obtain clear strikes.

The surface story changes — lights, bells, runners, wheels, devices or pendulums — but the underlying question stays the same:

When will these repeating cycles line up again?

Think L.C.M.

metadata.title: LCM in Repeating Events & Cyclic Problems
metadata.description: Use L.C.M. to find when repeating events coincide again and how many simultaneous occurrences happen in a stated duration.
